passage: The launch of the new tiffin-delivery route had failed: a sudden truckers' strike stopped supplies for four days, and half the orders were cancelled. Head office wanted someone to blame by evening. Indu, the operations lead, didn't open the complaints first. She opened the decision log she kept before every launch. Three weeks earlier she had written: "Go ahead. Supplier risk: low, 80% on time. Reason: two years of on-time deliveries. Unknown: union talks." She read it out to the team in the noisy warehouse. "Our reasoning was sound with what we knew. The unknown bit us. That's luck plus one blind spot." Payal, who had approved the supplier, finally looked up. Indu added, "Next time, someone tracks union news."

qa.q: What did Indu's log say was the unknown?
qa.a: The log said the unknown was union talks.

qa.q: Why did Payal finally look up when Indu read the log?
qa.a: Payal had approved the supplier and probably expected to be blamed; hearing that the reasoning was sound with what was known likely brought relief.

qa.q: Why does Indu's decision log make the review fairer?
qa.a: Because the forecast and reasons were written before the outcome, the team can separate a sound process from bad luck and find the one real gap, instead of blaming whoever signed.

qa.q: How might head office see Indu's answer?
qa.a: Head office wanted someone to blame, so they may be impatient at first, but a clear record of reasons and a specific fix gives them something more useful than a scapegoat.

grounding: Shows a mature lead using forecasts and reasons written before the outcome to separate process from luck, so no one is wrongly blamed.

passage: The quarterly review room in Koramangala was buzzing: the new pricing page had doubled sign-ups, and people wanted to praise Tenzin, who had pushed for it. Nirmala, the product lead, smiled but opened her forecast sheet first. Before launch, everyone had written a prediction and a reason. Tenzin's said: "Sign-ups +10%, because the page is simpler." Nirmala's own said +5%. "So none of us expected double," she said. "Let's check what actually happened." The data showed a festival sale that same week had brought huge traffic. "Good call, partly lucky timing," she told Tenzin warmly. "Your reason held up, though: the simpler page did convert better." Tenzin grinned, relieved to be judged on the reasoning, not just the number.

qa.a: Tenzin predicted sign-ups +10%, because the page is simpler.

qa.q: Why might Tenzin feel relieved to be judged on the reasoning?
qa.a: Being praised only for the doubled number would mean being blamed if luck turned; having the reasoning checked feels steadier and fairer.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's forecast sheet let the team learn from a success?
qa.a: It shows no one expected double, so they can separate the part caused by the festival sale from the part the simpler page earned, and learn the right lesson.

qa.q: How might the people who wanted to praise Tenzin see Nirmala's check?
qa.a: They might find it a little cautious at first, but later see that knowing what was luck stops the team from expecting double again next time.

grounding: Shows a lead comparing written forecasts with results to separate good reasoning from luck, even after a success.

passage: I'm Arohi, the woman who runs the kitchen at a small café in Pune, and last spring I learned to write things down before they happen. Kamal, our young cook, pitched a South Indian breakfast menu. Before saying yes, I opened a notebook and wrote: "Forecast: 60% chance breakfast sales rise within two months. Reasons: office crowd, no dosa place nearby. Risks: road work planned somewhere in our area, dates unknown." Then we launched. Six weeks later, the metro work closed our lane, and breakfast sales fell. The owner came in angry. "Whose idea was this?" Kamal went pale. I opened the notebook and showed him the page. "We knew about road work but not when. The idea was sound; the timing was bad luck." The owner read it twice. "Fine. Keep the menu, and check again after the lane opens." Kamal made me extra filter coffee that evening.

qa.q: What chance of success did Arohi write in her forecast?
qa.a: 60% chance breakfast sales rise within two months.

qa.q: Why did Kamal go pale when the owner asked whose idea it was?
qa.a: Kamal was afraid of being blamed for the fall in sales, since the menu was Kamal's idea and the result looked bad.

qa.q: What choice did Arohi make before the launch that protected the team later?
qa.a: She wrote down her forecast, reasons and risks before launching. That record let the review separate the sound decision from the bad luck of the lane closure.

qa.q: How might the owner see the menu decision after reading the notebook?
qa.a: The owner seems to move from anger to fairness, seeing the risk had been noted and the timing was out of their hands, so the menu gets another chance.

grounding: A café lead writes her forecast and reasons before a menu launch, so when luck turns bad the review judges the process, not the cook.

passage:
Regional coordinator's note, community radio network. Written by Damini, after visiting the Aizawl station.
Lalremsiami, the station lead, is twenty-five and does something none of our other leads do. Before any big change, she writes a one-page note: what she expects, how sure she is, and why. In March she moved the farmers' show from morning to evening. Her note said: "65% chance more listeners; farmers told us mornings are busy. Risk: evening power cuts." The move failed; listeners dropped by a third. In the review, two volunteers blamed her. She took out the note. The power cuts had doubled that month because of line repairs, which nobody had predicted. The reasoning had been sound. The team agreed to try again after the repairs, and no one was blamed. I watched her keep calm and I want every station to use her one-page note. I've sent the template to all six leads.

qa.a: From morning to evening.

qa.q: How do you think Lalremsiami felt when two volunteers blamed her, and what shows it?
qa.a: She may have felt stung, but she stayed calm and took out her note. Having written her reasons in advance let her face the review steadily.

qa.q: What did Damini decide to do after watching the review, and why?
qa.a: Damini sent Lalremsiami's one-page note template to all six station leads, so other reviews can separate good reasoning from bad luck.

qa.a: They may feel a bit embarrassed for blaming Lalremsiami, but also reassured that their own future decisions will be judged fairly.

The school-enrolment drive in Ward 9 flopped: 14 families signed up, and we'd hoped for 60. At the review, Mr Sen started with, "Farida should have known Ward 9 was difficult."

Joseph

passage: The farmer cooperative's office in Bankura smelled of jute sacks. This season's new paddy variety had failed on half the plots, and members were angry. "Preeti madam pushed this seed," someone shouted. "Anyone could see it was risky." Arnab, the secretary, didn't argue. He opened the red register where, every June, he wrote down each decision before sowing. He read aloud: "New variety on forty plots. Reason: resists the pest that hit us last year. Risk: needs steady rain. Rain forecast: normal. Our guess: good yield, seven chances in ten." He looked up. "The rain stopped for three weeks in August. None of us knew that in June." The room grew quieter. An old farmer nodded slowly. "Then next year, some plots old seed, some new." Preeti, at the back, finally unclenched her hands.

qa.q: What lesson did the old farmer draw, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: Planting some plots with old seed and some with new next year, which learns from the result without blaming anyone for luck.

qa.q: What might Preeti have felt as the room grew quieter?
qa.a: Preeti likely felt relieved, unclenching her hands once the register showed the blame was unfair.

grounding: A cooperative secretary reads out reasons and forecasts written before sowing, so a failed crop is reviewed without wrongly blaming the officer.

Hi team,

Before we launch the new delivery route next Monday, I'd like us to try something. In the shared sheet, please add:
1. What you expect to happen.
2. How confident you are (as a percentage).

passage:
You asked how I run reviews on my team, Akash. I'm Sumit, and I lead a small sales team at a furniture company. Here's the one habit that changed everything.

Before any big decision, like which city to open in or which client to chase, I write a short note. What we expect to happen. How sure we are. Why we think so. It takes five minutes.

Last year we opened in Nashik. I wrote, "60% chance this works. Main risk: a big competitor might arrive." Six months later, one did, and sales fell.

In the review, one manager said it was obvious we'd fail. I opened the note. "We said 60%. We named this risk. The decision was reasonable. We were unlucky." Nobody got blamed.

But in another case, the note showed we'd ignored a warning. That one, we learned from properly.

Without the notes, everything looks obvious afterwards.

qa.q: What chance of success did Sumit write for opening in Nashik?
qa.a: 60% chance this works.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel when the manager called the Nashik result obvious?
qa.a: Sumit felt calm and confident, because the note showed the decision had been reasonable and the risk was named.

qa.q: Why is writing forecasts before outcomes a fair practice?
qa.a: It shows what was known at the time, so reviews can separate bad luck from bad decisions and avoid wrongly blaming people.

qa.q: How might Sumit's team members feel about this habit?
qa.a: Team members probably feel safer taking reasonable risks, knowing they won't be blamed for bad luck.

grounding: A lead writes forecasts and reasons before decisions so later reviews separate luck from judgement and fewer people are blamed.

I work on Alka's project team at a publishing house. I'm Rukmini. I don't know everything Alka thinks, but I've watched how she runs things.

Before every book launch, she writes a short sheet: expected sales, how sure she is, and why. She pins it on the board. We all sign it.

Last spring, a travel book we all loved sold badly. At the review, the marketing head started saying, "Anyone could see that cover wouldn't work."

Alka took down the sheet. "In February we all agreed the cover was strong. We said 70% it would sell well. The reason it didn't was a rival book released the same week. We didn't know that."

The marketing head went quiet.

Then Alka asked, "What could we have known?" Someone pointed out that we could have checked other publishers' release dates. We added that to the checklist.

No one was blamed. I remember feeling relieved.

qa.q: What did Alka pin on the board before every book launch?
qa.a: A short sheet: expected sales, how sure she is, and why.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel at the end of the review?
qa.a: Rukmini felt relieved that no one was blamed and the team learned something useful.

qa.q: What did Alka's sheet make possible in the review?
qa.a: The sheet showed what the team knew in February, so the review could separate bad luck from a real gap, like checking rival release dates.

qa.q: How might the marketing head have felt when Alka read the February sheet?
qa.a: The marketing head may have felt caught out and a little embarrassed, having claimed anyone could see the cover wouldn't work.

Monday, early March. Noor, the new team lead at a Bengaluru app studio, started something odd. Before deciding whether to launch a new feature in April, she asked everyone to write down their guess and their reason in a shared file. Jahnavi wrote, "70% users will like it. Reason: beta testers were happy."

Friday, late April. The feature launched. Users hated it. Complaints flooded in. The CEO's first question was, "Who approved this?" Jahnavi felt sick. She'd pushed for it.

Wednesday, early May. At the review, Noor opened the March file. "Here's what we knew. The beta testers were happy. We were 70% sure. What changed was a new phone update that broke the layout. None of us knew that."

The CEO read it twice. "So the decision was sound. The luck was bad."

Jahnavi let out a breath. She hadn't been blamed. And the team added "check upcoming phone updates" to the launch list.

qa.a: Beta testers were happy.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when the CEO asked who approved the feature?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt sick and afraid of being blamed, because she had pushed for the launch.

qa.q: How did Noor's shared file protect the team and still help them learn?
qa.a: The file showed what was known in March, so the review separated bad luck from bad judgement and still found a lesson about phone updates.

qa.q: How might the CEO see the team after reading the March file?
qa.a: The CEO may trust the team's process more, seeing the decision was reasonable even though the outcome was bad.

grounding: Over two months, a lead records forecasts and reasons before a launch so the later review blames no one unfairly.

passage: Sabina, sit, the chai is still hot. You look the way I looked after my first bad review. When I was twenty-five, I ran the dispatch desk at a small garment unit in Tiruppur.
